clusters.name: Your grandfather Gordon's death, 1991–1992
clusters.reason: Around your grandfather Gordon dying in June 1991, within the year: your wrist injury stopped your playing and left you anxious and unable to function; you and Rafe came into conflict once you stopped playing, and you found yourself on your own, getting high and absorbed in fixing radios; by early 1992 you were lost and low, unable to get going with him gone and your mother about to remarry. Your mother filled in your college forms and you let it happen; your grandmother Winifred was treated for a thyroid tumour within a year of being widowed. The shifts in these months are yours and your grandmother's, and the events that pile up are your own reactions to the change in the family.

clusters.name: Your move to Gull Harbour, 2001–2004
clusters.reason: Around your move away from Thornbury in late 2002, within two years: you were running out of steam for performing and anxious by month; your grandmother Winifred was found to have bowel cancer in 2001 or 2002, with operations and chemotherapy alongside your disastrous audition; you left Thornbury for Gull Harbour and were on poor terms with family and friends; you met Marisol, moved to Fenwick to live with her, then split up within the year and sank into a deep depression once you were back in Thornbury that winter; you could not face your family, though you relied gingerly on friends—Corbin, Dale, and Hamish—and your grandmother spent her final months in your mother's home before she died in February 2004. Shifts pile up in the months around the move and the split, and your own trouble sits beside your grandmother's illness and death and your parents' distance from you.

clusters.name: Your grandmother Lorna's death, 2008
clusters.reason: Around your grandmother Lorna dying in January 2008, within months: you were too drained for conversation with your mother when you were at Alder Creek in July; she pressed to visit you and you kept the door shut on her; you left for nursing school in August and stopped speaking to your mother, a silence that held for roughly a year; your aunt Imogen had a stroke in January 2009 with months of rehabilitation ahead. The shift to cutoff with your mother sits with the death of your grandmother and your move away, and your aunt's illness follows close after.

clusters.name: Your marriage to Wren, 2017–2019
clusters.reason: Around your marriage to Wren in March 2017, within two years: you saw your mother a bit less once Wren came along; your cousin Alice was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her forties in October 2017; your sister Tara and her husband James married the previous summer and live in Rennick for her work; your aunt Imogen's memory slipped and worsened, and she lashed out when muddled; your cousin Leo returned to Danfield with his family in August 2019; your job steadied and paid well by June 2019, but you were constantly anxious that you ought to be driving your projects forward; you started a sleeping pill in October 2019 and began aiming for shorter, more regular calls with your mother. In late October 2019, Wren was swamped one thing after another around a street party, a fundraising dinner, and her mother's retirement party at the lake; you overfunctioned laying out a plan to settle her, and at the lake weekend you were awake from the small hours with no more sleep, could only pull back as the others rose, and felt you didn't belong; Wren was anxious when you'd had no sleep at family occasions. The shifts pile up around your marriage and Wren's entry into your family circle, with your own anxiety and her swamping side by side in the late weeks of October.

periods.name: the year I left home
periods.words: The first is the year I left home: I went off to the conservatory, hurt my wrist in the first term and couldn't play, dropped out and drifted at my mother's place, then spent a bleak spell at the community college shooting pool every night until an exchange in Portugal snapped me out of it and I tore through the rest of my coursework.

periods.name: the long slump
periods.words: The second is the long slump, roughly ages 27 to 29, when nothing at home felt right, I moved to Gull Harbour away from nearly everyone I knew, then followed Marisol to Fenwick, and when that fell apart I went under, a depression I only really climbed out of after nursing school.
